The complexities of service supervision: an experiential discovery

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin

120 Belsize Lane
London, NW3 5BA
UK

Margaret Rustin  

service supervision, method for studying supervision, supervisor role, splitting, multi-disciplinary team relationships, professional identity

Service supervision has become a central feature of the training of child psychotherapists in the UK. This paper reports on the work of a research workshop set up to explore the task and its complexities. The paper draws on several years of monthly meetings of a highly experienced group of supervisors. It discusses the methodology for studying supervisory processes, problems of confidentiality, the definition of role, the nature of the anxieties supervisors experience, splitting processes, which are a prominent phenomenon in the relationships between clinical placement supervisor and Training School staff, the trainee's and supervisor's relationship to the multi-disciplinary team, and the considerable pleasures and difficulties inherent in the service supervisor's task. The group was felt to be a creative experience and to enable us to discover much and to benefit from support.

Barbara Segal  

Clinical commentary by Barbara Segal, a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist working in University College London Hospitals

This moving clinical account describes the psychotherapeutic work undertaken in her hospital room with 13-year-old Maya, after the sudden onset of a terrifying and serious illness, Guillain–Barré syndrome, leaving her with paralysis and extreme weakness. The first session takes place almost three weeks after Maya's hospital admission and the second recorded session is the seventh, about five weeks later.

In the first meeting, the psychotherapist introduces him/herself and the service offered. Mother quite hastily leaves the room and the psychotherapist has the opportunity to hear from the patient about the onset of her illness and how she experienced this. Although Maya also tries to talk about the more ordinary aspects of her life and interests, she does convey her confusion and distress about her hospitalisation.

In the next meeting, the atmosphere is much changed. Maya's symptoms have worsened and she and mother are very tearful, trying not to show their distress to each other. The psychotherapist is required to bear some of the distress and to try to understand with Maya the fear and uncertainty that she is facing.

I shall look at the sessions in some detail, and discuss questions that arise in my mind. These are prompted by the clinical account here, which reflects some of the particular challenges and dilemmas that confront child and adolescent psychotherapists in paediatric liaison work in hospitals.

Paediatric liaison work

Child and adolescent psychotherapists working in hospitals are usually based within departments of psychological medicine within the hospital, offering a service in the areas of paediatrics and adolescent medicine. There are different models but mostly we work within the medical teams, functioning as an integral part of the multi-disciplinary medical specialities. The hospital, structured into wards, clinics, day care and outpatients, represents an ‘applied setting’. Nevertheless, psychoanalytic work is possible and very effective, with a heavy emphasis on flexibility and adaptability of our technique. Monica Lanyado writes about ‘an attentiveness to the setting of the treatment’, which involves a ‘tailor-made adaptation of the therapist's mind to the needs of the individual patient … rather than the patient having to adapt to the classical psychoanalytic model’ (Lanyado, 1996: 428).

Clinical commentary by Cathy Troupp, child and adolescent psychotherapist working at Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children, London

These sessions strikingly illustrate how therapeutic work with children with severe or life-threatening illnesses is so different from mainstream CAMHS work, and also how difficult this work can be.

It is one thing to address primitive anxieties, such as the fear of dying, with physically well children, and quite another to do so with children who may actually be dying, or who don't know whether they will be well again, or how long it may take. In well children, there is the background reassurance – comforting to both patient and therapist – that they aren't really dying just now. With seriously ill children, there is no such reassurance.

I think these two situations need to be seen as separate and different, with the bodily illness making all the difference. Although the fear of dying can feel very real to a well child who finds himself or herself in a psychically threatening situation of some kind, it can be jumped out of, and reality returned to, like waking up from a bad dream. But children who really are ill cannot wake up from the bad dream; hence the condition is like a ‘living nightmare’.

Review: long term psychodynamic psychotherapy improves outcomes in people with complex mental disorders

Paul Knekt, Olavi Lindfors & Maarit Laaksonen

Evidence Based Mental Health, 2009, 12 (2): 56, BMJ Publishing Group Ltd

Question: How effective is long term psychodynamic psychotherapy (LTPP) in people with complex mental disorders? Outcomes: Overall outcome, target problems, general psychiatric symptoms, personality and social functioning. Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis. Data sources: MEDLINE, PsycINFO and Current Contents were searched from 1960 to May 2008 for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies. Reference lists of identified articles and textbooks were hand searched, and authors and experts contacted for further information. Study selection and analysis: Two reviewers appraised the studies and selected RCTs and observational studies of LTPP. Inclusion criteria: studies in adults; ≥50 sessions or 1 year of LTTP; reliable outcome measures used; mental disorders of participants clearly described; and sufficient data to determine effect sizes. Studies with concomitant treatments were included but analysed separately to compare results of combined treatments versus LTTP alone. Two reviewers independently rated study quality, extracted data and assessed effect sizes. Point biserial correlation coefficients (rp) were used as measures of between and within group effect sizes.

As I read this book, my associations kept returning to the thoughts of a scientist whom I had read 30-plus years ago during a psychology class. The professor introduced the class to the work of Jacob Bronowski. The professor continued my introduction to Freud, to the stages of child development from the various schools or orientations, and highlighted each stage remarkable for its place in the mid-1970s period. He also focused our understanding of what the goals of psychotherapy were, as he was also a practising clinician.

It was this professor's insistence on our reading this short book of essays by Bronowski (Science and Human Values) that is most memorable. Bronowski's underlying theme throughout this work – and undoubtedly my professor's motivation – was ‘we must touch others’. Jacob Bronowski was a scientist and a humanist – but ‘touching others’ in the relational sense was a thread that ran through much of his work.

The parallel in this review is on the change possible within relationships. This excellent collection of work brought together by Tessa Baradon, aptly demonstrates, especially through the clinical illustrations, the need to touch others – to help those who have been so afflicted by trauma and traumatic circumstances that the relationship between a mother and an infant is deeply affected and in need of professional understanding and aid.

The researchers' contributions in this collection present their attempts to assess, to integrate and to document the diagnostic criteria that will be useful in furthering the clinical endeavour. The data also illustrates the efficacy of the clinician's work with these traumatised parents and infants. The focus is on the relationship – touching each other – and, as was underscored by Baradon and Bronfman, the capacity to increase our sensitivity to and understanding of the infant and parent in trouble – and enhancing our therapeutic efforts. Linda Mayes also highlights this constant thread in all the psychotherapeutic work discussed in the clinical and the research-oriented chapters, that is, the parent's ability to reflect on the emotional needs of the infant and importantly the understanding of how the parent's needs, wishes and behaviour ‘directly impact [the] infant's feelings and needs’.

Tessa Dalley  

Through assessment to consultation: independent psychoanalytic approaches with children and adolescents, edited by Ann Horne and Monica Lanyado, London, Routledge, 2009, 208 pp., £17.99

Drawing on the Independent tradition of psychoanalysis, this edited volume of 12 chapters explores the role of child psychotherapists who undertake assessment and consultation work in a variety of settings. Through assessment to consultation is not a handbook, but demonstrates the diversity of ways in which child psychotherapists are working indirectly with children and their families. The book introduces the idea of ‘assessment in progress’, assessment as a continuous thinking process towards reaching a formulation which is a working diagnosis. In the same way, consultation requires active thinking to heighten awareness of the unconscious dynamics operating within professional networks and staff teams.

The introduction, by the editors Ann Horne and Monica Lanyado, uses ideas from Winnicott to suggest that ‘we aim at being ourselves by keeping a compassionate clinical sense that does not abuse the analytic method even while we explore extremes of technique and understanding to wide range of settings’ (p. 4). Another way of putting it is that they are ‘doing something else’ or working as psychotherapists while not working directly with patients.

The book is organised into three sections, reflecting a continuum the editors see from assessment through to consultation.

Part one: assessment

The first section considers assessment for a number of different purposes and in a number of specialist settings. In chapter two, ‘Every assessment matters’, Mary Walker explains the child psychotherapist's role in assessment in child and adolescent mental health settings. This is a helpful description of the process, distinguishing core assessments and specialist assessments for individual child psychotherapy. Consideration is given to the role of the child psychotherapist within the assessment framework of the multi-disciplinary team because, as the author suggests, sometimes it is not clear to the ‘outsider’ that this role involves thinking from a psychoanalytic perspective, rather than being directly involved in the therapeutic work with a child. The ‘Anna Freud Diagnostic Profile’ was briefly mentioned and I was sorry that more was not made of the contribution it can make to a meta-psychological understanding of the child at this important assessment stage.

Clinical commentary

Clinical material

Background

Lewis is a six-year-old boy of mixed ethnicity. He lives with his maternal grandparents and has done so for the past five years. He has a younger brother who also lives with them.

The service where I work is an inner city CAMHS clinic. Lewis was referred to the service because of his unmanageable behaviour at home and at school. He has difficulty making friends and frequently displays aggressive behaviour towards others. He has also displayed sexualised behaviour at home and at school and the threat of exclusion from school is current.

Lewis's mother, Mary, was previously a heroin user. She is now engaged in a rehabilitation programme. At the time of the assessment for psychotherapy Lewis had regular contact, including overnight stays, with his mother and his mother's partner. Lewis has had no contact with his birth father for the past three years. Previous contact was supervised and via a contact centre, however, this ceased abruptly and father's whereabouts are unknown to the family.

The pregnancy with Lewis was unplanned and Mary's drug use worsened significantly during her pregnancy. Birth was by caesarean section and Lewis was born drug-addicted. Lewis and his mother lived together for the first eight months of his life. Mary then returned to using drugs when he was approximately 10 months old and he was placed in to his grandparents care. In the same year, maternal uncle dropped Lewis and he suffered a fracture. He was removed from his grandparents’ care and placed into foster care for five months, before returning to live with them.

The session presented here is the second of three psychotherapy assessment sessions with Lewis. There was considerable uncertainty as to whether psychotherapy should be offered as it did not feel that Lewis's external environment was a safe enough context for him to be able to explore his feelings. I and a colleague (who had been offering monthly appointments to Lewis's grandparents) referred Lewis and his brother to Children's Social Care during the psychotherapy assessment. This referral has since been taken up and Lewis's contact with his mother now takes place under supervision. Lewis subsequently received a psychiatric assessment within this service. One of the recommendations of the psychiatric report has been for Lewis’ grandparents to receive regular appointments with a psychotherapist from within the service in order to explore their capacities to support a psychotherapy treatment for Lewis.

Clinical commentary by Biddy Youell, head of child psychotherapy at Tavistock Centre, London

Biddy Youell

Biddy Youell

120 Belsize Lane
London, NW3 5BA
UK

Biddy Youell  

Clinical commentary by Biddy Youell, head of child psychotherapy at Tavistock Centre, London

Lewis's history is sadly all too familiar to child psychotherapists working in CAMHS and even more so in specialist services for looked-after children. It is hard for clinicians not to have the full horror of the child's external reality in the front of their mind when thinking about the internal reality as revealed in the therapy room. There is obviously a question about his experience of being born heroin-addicted and the long-term neurological effects of going through withdrawal as an infant … as well as the emotional and psychological impact of living with a heroin-addicted mother for the first eight months of his life. Being moved from her care to his grandparent's home, and then back and forth into foster care when he was dropped by an uncle, adds to the trauma which he suffered in the pre-verbal phase of his development.

This is only the second assessment session, a fact I completely lost sight of when reading the process notes. Lewis is so deeply into the session and is treating the room and the therapist as if he has been there forever. The way in which he catapulted himself into the session reminded me of his having been born by caesarean section and moved immediately into special care. There was no ordinary birth process and at best, an interrupted introduction to his mother. The session begins in the waiting room with Lewis reacting to the sight of another therapist with another child. There seems to be an edge of mockery in his imitation of the other therapist, maybe a way of splitting to keep his own therapist ‘good’ in his mind.

The key communication in this session occurs right at the beginning when the therapist attempts to comment on his agitated state of mind. “No, I don't get worried.” These words speak volumes in a boy who goes on to show some of the many ways in which he tries to make sure that he does not feel any worry. It also seems to carry a bit of a warning to the therapist that if she is going to try to make him worried, she will not succeed. He tells her that what she is offering (toys) is ‘rubbish’ and spins off to the sink. She is able to help him at this point with her comment about cooling down and he responds with his wish to wash away the red (anger? danger?).

Author biographies

Anne Alvarez (Ph.D.) is a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist and retired Co-Convener of the Autism Service at the Tavistock Clinic. Anne is a Visiting Professor at the San Francisco Psychoanalytic Society. Anne is widely published: author of Live Company: Psychotherapy with Autistic, Borderline, Deprived and Abused Children (2002, Routledge) joint editor with Sue Reid of, Autism and Personality: Findings from the Tavistock Autism Workshop (1999, Routledge). Her work is the subject of Being Alive: Building on the Work of Anne Alvarez (Ed Edwards, J.) (2001, Routledge).

Paddy Martin. For the last seven years, Paddy Martin has worked at the North Middlesex Hospital Paediatric Liaison Team and has an interest in psychosomatic presentation and illness, as well as the emotional impact of acute and chronic illness stretching back to even earlier work in nursing and rehabilitation work with blind and partially sighted people. For the last three years, he has worked for the Court Assessment Service at the Anna Freud Centre and developed an interest in the intergenerational impact and transmission of attachment patterns and the link between parents with personality disorders and disorganised attachment.

He also teaches a module on intergenerational transmission of attachment for the Parent-Infant Project at the Anna Freud Centre, as well as a series of seminars on Psychosomatic Disorders for the third-year trainees at the British Association of Psychotherapy.

Claudia McLoughlin is a child and adolescent psychotherapist who qualified from the Tavistock Centre in January 2002. Since then she has worked within the Islington CAMHS Service. Having been a special needs teacher before her therapeutic training, Claudia has a particular interest in working in partnership with alternative educational settings in trying to reach socially excluded and marginalised young people and their families. She is also interested in the creative use of work discussion groups in various community settings, and in group psychotherapy for children, in parallel with psychodynamic parent group treatment. Claudia is currently exploring the possibility of making more explicit connections between her therapeutic and meditation practice, as well as between Buddhist and psychoanalytic ways of looking at life and the world.

Author biographies

Simonetta M.G. Adamo is Professor of Clinical Psychology at the University of Milan, Bicocca. She is a child and adolescent psychotherapist, member of the Tavistock Society of Psychotherapists and has taught on many Tavistock model observation courses in Italy. She has published papers in academic journals internationally, and has contributed to and edited many books on topics such as adolescence, psychodynamic counselling, Asperger's syndrome, the imaginary companion, young child observation, projects aimed at improving child and adolescent mental health in educational contexts, and psychotherapy in paediatric oncology wards. For the past 15 years, she has been co-organising tutor of the short course ‘Working with disruptive adolescents’ held at the Tavistock Clinic.

Louise Allnutt is a child and adolescent psychotherapist who works in a child development team with children who have complex disabilities, and an inner city CAMHS clinic that specialises in court assessments. She trained at the Tavistock Clinic, where she now also teaches on courses in Infant Mental Health and Psychoanalytic Observation Studies.

Maggie Fagan is a child and adolescent psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic where she is a member of the Fostering, Adoption and Kinship Care Team and also co-convener of the Fostering and Adoption Workshop. She has a specialist interest in late adoption. She is also the assessment tutor and liaison tutor on the Observational Studies Course at the Tavistock Clinic.

Pasqual J. Pantone, PhD, is Director of Clinical Education, Fellow, Training and Supervising Analyst in the Psychoanalytic Division of the William Alanson White Institute in New York. He is also former co-director and co-founder of the Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy Training Program at the William Alanson White Institute. He is a supervisor at the Northwest Center for Psychoanalysis in Portland, Oregon. He is co-author of Relational Child Psychotherapy (2002), published by Other Press.

Margaret Rustin is a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist at the Tavistock and Portman NHS Foundation Trust. She was head of the child psychotherapy training for 21 years and thus closely involved in the process of closer integration of the training with NHS services through the commissioning of training. She remains deeply interested in the clinical and intellectual challenges of the changing training context.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Viviane Green and Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley  

In the UK, many trainees have NHS-funded posts and are able to undertake their training in a Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service where their training needs are overseen by the service supervisor and, as Margaret Rustin points out, ‘Service supervision has become a central feature of the training of child psychotherapists in the UK’. Her paper reports on the work of a research workshop set up to explore the task and its complexities. The workshop ran for several years of monthly meetings and was attended by a highly experienced group of supervisors. It was able to address the many issues arising out of the supervisor's complex role in supporting, managing and supervising the trainee. The article also looks at the potential problems inherent in the supervisor's role given that the trainee is also being supervised by the Training School's supervisor. The movement between a trainee and the supervisor managing ‘seamless’ relationships or split ones makes for fascinating reading. This is the first time the Journal of Child Psychotherapy has published an article in this area and is a significant contribution to the profession. We hope that it will also stimulate further contributions on the role of the supervisor working in different contexts.

The 2008 essay prize, awarded in 2009, was for a qualifying paper. We received a large number of entries and, in this issue, we are publishing two excellent papers that reflect rather different ways of working. Both therapists (in Strati's words) think of the therapeutic task as lying in ‘capturing the hope that maybe someone could manage and process what feels unbearable and unthinkable, but also the fear that no one can or will.’

Katerina Strati's paper, ‘Peek-a-boo. How can you be there? Analytic work with a severely traumatised two-and-a-half-year-old girl’, asks some difficult and interesting questions about working with very early trauma. Phoebe had witnessed her mother killing her father, Phoebe's grandfather. ‘While it is widely established that trauma occurring in the pre-verbal period can significantly impact on the child's physiological development and psychic organisation (Perry, 1995; Shore, 2001), it is less clear whether and how the traumatic experience is registered, represented and remembered,’ Strati writes. The paper vividly shows how the layers of developmental damage, non-verbal and gradually verbalised elements all come into the treatment relationship.

Children's actions when experiencing domestic violence

Carolina Överlien & Margareta Hydén

Childhood, 2009, Volume 16 (4): 479–96

The aim of this article is, by analysing children's discourses, to investigate their actions or absence of actions during a domestic violence episode. The empirical data are recorded group therapy sessions and individual interviews with children who have grown up experiencing their fathers’ violence against their mothers. The analysis shows that the children's stories contain two aspects of actions: one related to the actions during the ongoing episode, and one the child perceives as possible/desirable for the future. The findings are discussed in the light of Lazarus and Folkman's theory of coping.

Mentalisation in children exposed to parental methamphetamine abuse: relations to children's mental health and behavioural outcomes

Teresa Ostler, Ozge Sensoy Bahar & Allison Jessee

Attachment and Human Development, May 2010, Volume 12 (3): 193–207

This study examined the mentalisation capabilities of children exposed to parental methamphetamine abuse in relation to symptom underreporting, mental health and behavioural outcomes. Twenty-six school-aged children in foster care participated in this study. Mentalisation was assessed using the My Family Stories Interview, a semi-structured interview in which children recalled family stories about a happy, sad or scary and fun time. An established scale of the Trauma Symptom Checklist for Children, a self-report measure, provided information on children's symptom underreporting. The Child Behavior Checklist, completed by the children's foster caregivers, assessed children's mental health and behavioural outcomes. Children with higher mentalisation were significantly less prone to underreport symptoms. These children had fewer mental health problems and were rated by their foster caregivers as more socially competent. The findings underscore that mentalisation could be an important protective factor for children who have experienced parental substance abuse.

Mary Target  

The psychoanalytic work of Hansi Kennedy: from war nurseries to the Anna Freud Centre (1940–1993)

The psychoanalytic work of Hansi Kennedy: from war nurseries to the Anna Freud Centre (1940–1993), edited by Jill M. Miller and Carla Neely, London, Karnac, 2008, 306 pp., £29.99, ISBN 13: 978-1-85575-523-9

It has been difficult to stand back from this book on Hansi Kennedy, skilfully edited by Jill Miller and Carla Neely, two of her very able students who have returned to the United States and had distinguished careers there as leading child analysts. Hansi Kennedy was someone it was best to know, work with, live with, to get her measure as she was not one – the editors point out – to blow her own trumpet. She did not write or present many papers of her own, and seemed much happier contributing to a group or helping young colleagues get going by writing something together. I was one who had the privilege of being helped in that spirit, as a research psychologist at the Anna Freud Centre 20 years ago, an outsider she could easily have ignored. After collaborating on a minor paper together, we wrote two much more substantial pieces in a group that worked and wrote together regularly for six years (Rose Edgcumbe, Hansi Kennedy, George Moran, Peter Fonagy and myself). We contributed a theoretical paper on child psychopathology and technique for the annual Colloquium (Fonagy et al., 1993), and a book on the theory and technique of child analysis at the Centre, which we never published. This was partly because Hansi felt it was not really her or our work, or the Centre's collective work; we represented the Centre's tradition and approach using many examples from colleagues seen and understood through the eyes of our group; it was best left as a resource for scholars and clinicians, and that is what we have let it be. It was typical of Hansi in my experience, to devote many hundreds of hours of work but be genuinely uninterested in taking credit, or even particularly in seeing the work presented, the point was to think and learn something, and work it through in the group. Others might be interested and could take what they wished, but she would not push it at them. I always felt that she was solid and secure in her experience and clear in her own interests, but that she felt no need to try to persuade others to be like her.

Author biographies

Dimitris C. Anagnostopoulos (M.D, Ph.D.) is child and adolescent psychiatrist and psychoanalytic psychotherapist and a member of the Hellenic Association of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy. Since 2005 he has been the Chair of the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Section of the World Psychiatric Association. He is Assistant Professor of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry of the University of Athens, and Director of Child and Adolescent Mental Health Unit, 1st Psychiatric Department, Athens University Medical School. He is the author and co-author of more than 140 published scientific papers.

Dimitris Anastasopoulos (M.D, Ph.D.) is a training psychoanalytic psychotherapist and supervisor working with adults, adolescents and children. He was trained in Athens and at the Tavistock Clinic in London. His main interest is adolescence. He is a founding member of the Hellenic Association of Child and Adolescent Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy and for the last eight years he has been Vice Chair and Co-ordinator of the Child and Adolescent Section of the European Federation of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy (EFPP). He has written numerous articles and book chapters, and is co-editor and contributing author to three books published by Karnac, London: Countertransference in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy with Children and Adolescents, 1996; Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy of Severely Disturbed Adolescents, 1999; The Therapist at Work. Personal Factors Affecting the Analytic Process, 2004. He is currently also chief editor of a new EFPP series.

Saralea E. Chazan (Ph.D.) is a clinical psychologist practising in Greenwich Village, New York City. She is an invited researcher in the Steinhardt School, New York University and a research associate at the Pacella Parent Child Center, The New York Psychoanalytic Institute.

Esther Cohen (Ph.D.) is a faculty member and the former head of the Child-Clinical Psychology Program at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel. She is an accredited specialist and supervisor in Clinical Psychology, Developmental Psychology and Family Therapy. Her publications on trauma are based on 30 years of clinical work and research with children and families, victims of war and violence in Israel. While on sabbatical in NYC during 2001–2, she consulted to a number of centres as part of the relief efforts in the aftermath of 9/11.

On not being able to enter Noah's Ark

Simonetta Adamo

Simonetta Adamo

Bicocca, Italy

Simonetta Adamo  

psychoanalytic psychotherapy, high-functioning Asperger's syndrome, conventional versus intimate relationships, Meltzerian theory, beauty

The paper describes the psychoanalytic psychotherapy of a patient who had originally been referred at the age of 15 because of his social isolation. In fact, he suffered from high-functioning Asperger's syndrome and lived in an almost delusional world populated by a number of imaginary companions, which he used to counteract a deep void and sense of deadliness within him. After five years of therapy, the patient was able to move on, allowing him to be successful in his academic studies, and to abandon his imaginary friends. This paper focuses on a subsequent phase of the therapy when the patient, as a young man, began to show an interest in and attraction to the world of intimate relationships. The paper is grounded in Meltzerian theory, especially his ideas about the role of beauty in the mother–child relationship, and about the world of intimate links as opposed to conventional ones.

[[RunningHead]]

The damaged object: a ‘strange attractor’ in the dynamical system of the mind

Graham Shulman

Graham Shulman

194 Quarry Street
Hamilton, Lanarkshire ML3 6QR
UK

Graham Shulman  

the damaged object, relation to reality, internal and external reality, chaos theory, nonlinearity, strange attractor, iteration, recursion

This article discusses the impact of the damaged object on the development and functioning of psychic life with particular reference to the sense of reality. The damaged object is of pivotal significance in Klein's and Winnicott's models of psychic development and experience in early infancy. A key dimension of the development and functioning of the sense of reality is the capacity to differentiate internal and external reality. Klein drew attention to the critical role of external reality in disconfirming or ‘disproving’ phantasies and anxieties about damaged objects in internal reality, and Winnicott emphasised the critical importance to psychic health and development of the ‘non-destruction’ of the external object. Problems can arise, however, when external reality has the effect of mirroring or confirming – instead of disconfirming – internal reality concerning the damaged object. The scientific concept of the ‘strange attractor’ from chaos theory is drawn on to characterise the way in which the damaged object can operate as a deterministic influence on psychic life and the relationship to reality in a specific constellation of internal and external realities. In this context, the relevance of chaos theory is considered as a scientific paradigm that is particularly suited to the psychoanalytic description and model of the mind. Some possible links between psychoanalysis, chaos theory and the study of narrative are explored. Detailed clinical material from two cases is discussed to elaborate these themes, and possible research applications are considered.

Clinical material

Background

Carol is an 11-year-old girl of mixed British and Caribbean origin. She was adopted at age one, as her teenage mother, who had been in care herself and was a drug user, could not look after her. Carol was born prematurely and spent a few weeks in an incubator. During her first year, she was in foster care with attempts at rehabilitation with her birth mother. Mr and Mrs A. adopted Carol as their first child. Mr A. is originally from the Caribbean and Mrs A. is British. They present as a trendy, well-to-do couple who deal with the difficulties around their daughter by becoming the experts themselves. Carol has an adoptive sister, three years younger than her, whose adoption was described as extremely successful.

Carol was a complacent young child who showed no separation difficulties from her foster parents, but was found to have problems forming a good attachment to her adoptive parents. She was referred to the clinic by a post-adoption social worker at age seven. The parents reported that she could barely express loving feelings towards them and had an attitude of not caring much about them. She sometimes expressed emotions by enacting playing as a cat. Carol was wetting and soiling the bed, had sleeping difficulties, had no friendships in school, was aggressive towards her sister and was found to speak in often confused ways, in that the content of her speech was disorienting and disconnected. Worryingly, she frequently went up to strangers, showing no anxiety. Her parents had a tendency to downplay her difficulties as being a sign of an eccentric and interesting personality. Carol's sister on the other hand was described as a highly intelligent, sensitive girl who fitted into the family perfectly. Inevitably, there is a lot of rivalry between the siblings.

Before being referred for intensive therapy, a colleague saw Carol for two years of once-weekly therapy and the period of work ended because the therapist left the clinic. Carol herself asked to come back to the clinic and it was felt that she needed intensive work in order to address her deep-seated difficulties.

Diagnosis, disclosure and having autism: an interpretive phenomenological analysis of the perceptions of young people with autism

Jaci Huws & Robert S.P. Jones

Journal of Intellectual and Developmental Disability, June 2008, Volume 33 (2): 99–107, Informa Healthcare

Although there is extensive research examining parental experiences of assessment and diagnosis of autism, there is a paucity of research from the perspective of individuals with autism. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with nine young people with high functioning autism who were capable of providing a verbal account of their perceptions of autism and diagnosis experiences. Data were analysed using interpretative phenomenological analysis. Diagnosis, and the disclosure of the diagnosis of autism, were embedded in respondents' perceptions of ‘having’ autism. This superordinate theme included five themes: (i) disclosure delay, (ii) providing explanations, (iii) potential effects of labelling, (iv) disruptions and opportunities, and (v) acceptance and avoidance. In relation to the existing literature, it is suggested that the effects of diagnosis, or disclosure of diagnosis, from the perspective of the person with autism be given greater consideration.

Evidence based assessment of autism spectrum disorders in children and adolescents

Sally Ozonoff, Beth L. Goodin-Jones & Marjorie Solomon

Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology, August 2005, Volume 34 (3): 523–40, Routledge

This article reviews evidence-based criteria that can guide practitioners in the selection, use, and interpretation of assessment tools for autism spectrum disorders (ASD). As Mash and Hunsley (2005) discuss in this special section, evidence-based assessment tools not only demonstrate adequate psychometric qualities, but also have relevance to the delivery of services to individuals with the disorder (see also Hayes, Nelson and Jarrett, 1987). Thus, we use what is known about the symptoms, etiologies, developmental course, and outcome of ASD to evaluate the utility of particular assessment strategies and instruments for diagnosis, treatment planning and monitoring, and evaluation of outcome. The article begins with a review of relevant research on ASD. Next we provide an overview of the assessment process and some important issues that must be considered. We then describe the components of a core (minimum) assessment battery, followed by additional domains that might be considered in a more comprehensive assessment.

Editorial

Viviane Green and Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley  

This edition of the Journal of Child Psychotherapy offers a wide range of articles. The first two articles are on adolescence. The first is a psychoanalytically based account of outreach work with pregnant adolescent mothers and the second an original look at constructions of adolescence through ancient and modern myths. These are followed by two research-based articles, one from a primarily attachment-based perspective and the other from a psychoanalytic perspective.

Anne Hurley's ‘Reparation by proxy: experiences of working with pregnant teenagers and adolescent mothers’, describes brief interventions with pregnant teenagers, adolescent mothers, their infants and their wider families. She puts forward the interesting view that the adolescent who has herself experienced failure in her primary relationship with her mother may seek to repair this by becoming a mother herself but whilst still at a stage when her own identity is forming. The second clinical example of the daughter who ‘soaks in’ the experience of watching her own mother in the act of mothering her daughter is a vivid image of the ‘experience by proxy’, trying to capture that which had been missed.

Anastasopoulos et al. contribute an unusual and distinctive article about myth and mythologising and its relevance in adolescence. The inspiration that Freud derived from ancient Greek mythology comes alive in their interesting and comparative exploration of myth, mystical wisdom, fairy tale and ritual. They use a wide lens to consider representations of unconscious life in narratives of all kinds before homing in on myth and mythologising in particular. Using a fascinating weave of myths from ancient and contemporary times, they argue that myths convey enduring societal perceptions or perhaps misperceptions about adolescents. There is a theme throughout the article of myth containing elemental and facilitative messages of importance to adolescents as they negotiate transition to adulthood. Three clinical vignettes are included, which demonstrates the clinician working on the unravelling of myth and distortions of truth to good effect.

Work discussion: learning from reflective practice in work with children and families, edited by Margaret Rustin and Jonathan Bradley, London, Karnac, 2008, 309 pp., £19.99

Work discussion, as a topic, has been a Cinderella in the literature of child psychotherapy. This welcome volume, in the Tavistock Clinic Series, starts to fill out a substantial space. Work discussion, along with infant observation and individual and group supervision, is a central feature of child psychotherapy training, together with academic teaching. To date, it has had much less formal consideration than its fellows, although, to a lesser extent, the contribution of child psychotherapy to supervisory practice in training and beyond has also received insufficient attention. Yet as Trudy Klauber remarks in her short foreword to this book: ‘the work discussion model is the epitome of the application of psychoanalytic ideas’.

The concise foreword sticks to task in foreshadowing, in an engaging and interesting way, that which the editors will illustrate most successfully in the various sections of the book. Klauber outlines the psychoanalytic pre-history to the work discussion method, recalling the work of psychoanalytic luminaries such as Bion, Rickman, Balint, Bick, Anna Freud and the Robertsons. The broad applicability of the work discussion method is described, as is its transformative potential for individuals. Certain key concepts such as containment and projection are picked out.

Margaret Rustin, introducing the book, suggests that ‘Studies in Containment’ might have been an alternative title, so centrally did Bion's concept figure in a trawl of student archived work. The impact of Bion's work impresses the reader too, when one appreciates the theoretical underpinning his work on groups provides throughout this account of work discussion. This work on groups became widely disseminated and taught post-war in academic settings and vocational trainings, as did the applied work of other psychoanalysts with children in separation, or with GP groups, for example, and created much interest in the contributions of psychoanalysis. The account of current practice in work discussion at the Tavistock is firmly embedded in an historical perspective and links between past and present are one of its finely traced dimensions.

Clinical material

Background

Maya is 13 years old, and from a Hindu family. Father owns a business near the teaching hospital and mother supports him in the business and looks after the home. Maya is the youngest child and has an older sibling at university. Maya was due to start at an expensive and prestigious private school in a few months. Maya is intelligent and particularly gifted in maths. Her parents were thrilled that she had gained a place at this school and mother had said to the consultant that she was proud that they had been able to give their children such a privileged education. Six days before she was due to begin her new school Maya was taken ill with Guillain–Barré syndrome: a disorder in which the body's immune system attacks part of the peripheral nervous system. The first symptoms of this disorder include varying degrees of weakness or tingling sensations in the legs. In many instances, the weakness and abnormal sensations spread to the arms and upper body. These symptoms can increase in intensity until the muscles cannot be used at all and the patient is almost totally paralysed. In these cases, the disorder is life-threatening and is considered a medical emergency. The patient is often put on a respirator to assist with breathing. Most patients recover from even the most severe cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome, although some continue to have some degree of weakness. Maya was admitted to the teaching hospital four days after her symptoms appeared.

Maya's first session

I arrive at 12; Maya is just finishing her physiotherapy session. Mother invites me in and I sit on the visitor's bed close to where Maya is seated in a large armchair. Maya half smiles at me, and I introduce myself and say that I am from the CAMHS team and that we are part of the team who care for Maya on R ward and I could offer her some counselling time. I say that she spoke with D (our lead nurse) about this. Maya nods in understanding. Mother is talking quietly to the physiotherapist who is just about to leave the room and I am wondering if mother is going to stay and how to approach this, when mother turns around and says she will leave us for a while. I notice mother seems quite upset and I wonder if she is needing her own space. Before mother leaves, she gives Maya a drink from a bottle with a straw in it. I notice mother needs to hold the bottle as, although Maya has lifted her right hand up, her grip is weak. Mother gently strokes Maya's face and leaves us.

Music in the head, living at the mind-brain border, by Leo Rangell, M.D., London, Karnac, 2009, 93 pp., £14.99

This short book describes an account of an extraordinary life-change experienced by the author, one that was challenging, full of surprises and in many ways inspiring to readers. There is no doubting the credentials of the author, Dr Leo Rangell, who is a leading figure in American psychoanalysis, a former President of both the American and International Psychoanalytic Associations, and author of eight books and over 500 papers. No previous publication of his, though, will approach this in terms of the kind of story told, its personal nature and the likelihood to appeal to people well outside our field.

At the age of 82, Dr Rangell began to experience a range of symptoms that reminded him of previous cardiac problems, and major heart surgery ensued, after which he began to experience symptoms that meant that his life would never be the same again. His descriptions are throughout told with a sharp mind, an analytic ear and a capacity to convey personal experiences in an engaging way. He combines both autobiographical story-telling and a descriptive style in the best traditions of psychoanalytic case-history writing. He manages all this in a way that suggests an enormous amount of processing and thoughtful analysis has taken place, albeit with himself playing the parts of both patient and analyst.

He describes awakening from his operation with a range of semi-hypnotic and hallucinatory experiences, as one might expect following such a major event and with the kind of anaesthetic drugs used. He soon also realised he was hearing music, which he was convinced came from a building on a nearby hillside. It took a huge amount of persuading from his closest family and others before he had to admit that the incessant musical accompaniment heralded not from anywhere outside himself, but from somewhere inside his own mind, a truth that he strongly resisted at first. He was from that point onwards to experience such musical accompaniment for the rest of his life, and understood that he had become a scientific oddity, a case study, which might remind the reader of the kind of cases that Oliver Sacks describes. Indeed, fittingly Sacks is the author of the book's introduction.

Judith Mitrani  

autism, empathy, Frances Tustin, mirror neurons, psychoanalysis

This paper offers an integrative approach to the increasingly complex puzzle of autistic spectrum disorders. The author demonstrates how the work of one group of neuroscientists in Parma, on a special class of brain cells called ‘mirror neurons', and the work of researchers at the University of California in San Diego, applying these findings to the problem of autism, intersect with Frances Tustin's discoveries about the nature, function and meaning of psychogenic autism in children and even autistic states in neurotic adults. Included in the author's considerations are the results of some by now well-known studies conducted by a group of biologists at the University of California at Berkeley in the 1960s on the effects of ‘enriched’ versus ‘deprived’ environments upon the development of the brain, and a study of autistic children diagnosed as brain damaged and treated psychoanalytically at the Paediatric Neuro-Psychiatric Institute of the University of Rome in the 1980s. The author concludes with a coherent picture of various dimensions of autistic phenomenon that may constitute more than just the sum of its parts, and points towards new areas for discussion and study.

This article aims to reflect on the lessons learnt from using a psychodynamic approach to offering onsite therapeutic child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) in four pupil referral units (henceforth referred to as PRUs). The PRUs cater for six- to 16-year-old children and adolescents permanently excluded from mainstream schools. The work takes place in an inner London borough. The approach described evolved over five years through practice-based evidence of what worked well in each particular setting. This was viewed both in terms of sustaining families' engagement in the therapeutic process, and also effectively supporting child and adolescent mental health services and education staff in their respective tasks. The model which gradually evolved owes much to Bion's concept of containment as the necessary foundation for emotional growth and genuine learning. It also draws on ideas from psychoanalytic consultation and open systems theory. The importance of work discussion groups in this setting will also be evident. Some links are made to relevant Buddhist concepts and metaphors.

[[RunningHead]]

Adolescence and mythology

Dimitris Anastasopoulos , Eugenia Soumaki and Dimitris Anagnostopoulos

Dimitris Anagnostopoulos

Athens, 15451
Greece

Dimitris Anagnostopoulos  

Greek mythology, mythological thinking, adolescence, myths

The article begins with a brief exploration of the various aspects of adolescent's psychic qualities as these are described in Greek mythology. It is argued that myths are an integral part of the way that adolescence is perceived and myths play an important role in adolescents' psychic and external world, as well as in their mythological thinking. Connections are made with the attraction towards the creation of myths about adolescence in ancient and contemporary societies. Three clinical vignettes from adolescents' psychoanalytic psychotherapy are presented in an effort to support the idea of the value and importance of mythology in adolescence in the clinical practice. Through the clinical material, we try to explore how psychic and developmental disturbances, which might lead to psychopathology, are reflected in family and personal myths and also in the mythological thinking of adolescents.

Thoughts about the session material

This clinical extract raises many important issues for the child psychotherapist working with seriously ill children in hospital.

My countertransference to the first paragraph was to feel shock at the self-destructiveness of Guillain–Barré syndrome: how, like a cancer, the body's immune system attacks part of the nervous system. Furthermore, I was struck by how much uncertainty about the prognosis must surround Maya and her family. And I wondered why Maya's dramatic illness happened just at the point of her achieving academic success. But I realised that to think psychogenically was unhelpful, especially as this is not a ‘neurotic’ illness as far as we know.

At the beginning of the first session, the therapist acknowledges to Maya the length of time that she has been in hospital, summarises the worrying physical symptoms and succinctly refers to the timing of the onset of illness in the young girl's life. This ‘introduction’ by the psychotherapist is helpful, because it relieves the patient, who is already debilitated, of having to tell the story.

The question of normal sexuality begins to arise in the treatment of severely sexually abused or sexually offending patients. The author suggests that it is an interesting and delicate moment during the process of recovery when less perverse, more normal sexuality appears mixed with, or even disguised by, the more habitual perverse fantasies. Writers in the adult field have drawn distinctions between perverse, eroticized and normal erotic transferences, and between Oedipal and post-Oedipal sexuality. Some have also distinguished between countertransferences in the analyst of an erotised versus a normal erotic nature. The paper discusses whether these distinctions could have any relevance for child patients. Freud and Klein have taught us much about the child's sexuality in relation to his interest in and attraction

[[RunningHead]]

Adaptive and defensive strategies in post-traumatic play of young children exposed to violent attacks

Saralea Chazan and Esther Cohen

Esther Cohen

2 Fifth Ave
New York, New York 10011
USA

Esther Cohen  

play, trauma, coping, violence, resilience

Twenty-three children, aged four to eight years, who had been exposed to violent attacks, were videotaped in individual 40-minute play sessions. These play narratives were recorded by a student researcher trained in narrative analysis and play therapy. She then sorted these play vignettes into three patterns of post-traumatic play, defined in the Children's Play Therapy Instrument/Adaptation for Trauma Research (CPTI/ATR). The three patterns were re-enactment with soothing; re-enactment without soothing; and overwhelming re-enactment. Each pattern was analysed further by the student researcher and the two authors of the scale to specify in detail the qualitative features of each pattern. Factors leading to resilience are identified and the contribution of play activity to repair is discussed.

[[RunningHead]]

An activating mechanism of aggressive behaviour in disorganised attachment: a moment-to-moment case analysis of a three-year-old

Eun Kim

Eun Kim

39420 Liberty Street
Fremont, CA 94538
USA

Eun Kim  

aggressive behaviour, disorganised attachment, ambiguous situations, play therapy, a dual process, moment-to-moment analysis

This study examines an activating mechanism of aggressive behaviour in young children. Many studies on attachment theories have indicated disorganised attachment as a significant risk factor for externalising problems and have explained the aetiology of disorganised attachment in terms of deficits in affect, behaviour and cognitive functions from a traumatic or inconsistent environment. Via the moment-to-moment analysis of the play therapy process with a three-year-old, this paper attempts to identify how these emotional, behavioural and cognitive factors interact in actual situations and can lead to an observable behaviour: aggressive behaviour. The findings from this study indicate that the child with disorganised attachment was going through a dual process, one with her therapist and the other with her internalised caregivers. When anxiety and an ambiguous social cue from an unpredictable situation were added to the child's repetition of previous attachment experience, this ‘click’ lowered the threshold of regulation of affect, behaviour and cognition. The child turned to disorganised and aggressive behaviour, relying on her physiological signals regarding the perceived threat. Finally, this paper describes how these difficulties can be channelled by symbolic play via displacement and containment.

This paper shows a child psychotherapist learning and developing her technique as she attempts to make contact with a child who is extremely hard to reach. It is based on the first two years of three-times-weekly intensive psychotherapy of a latency girl who had little faith in a helpful therapeutic relationship. Theory and practice in child psychoanalysis: an introduction to the work of Françoise Dolto

Theory and practice in child psychoanalysis: an introduction to the work of Françoise Dolto, edited by Guy Hall, Françoise Hivernel and Sian Morgan, London, Karnac, 2009, 224 pp., £22.95, ISBN 978-1-85575-574-1

The title of this book is slightly misleading. It seems to suggest that what is being offered is a general survey of child psychoanalytic theory and practice with particular reference to the work of the French psychoanalyst, Françoise Dolto. In reality, it consists of a detailed exposition of her life, work and theories (not all of these directly bearing on child psychoanalysis), with only passing mention made of other significant figures in the field, such as Melanie Klein, Anna Freud and Donald Winnicott. Its authors' hope, one supposes, is to have her name eventually added to this august trinity.

Who, then, was Françoise Dolto? Since most English-speaking child analysts and psychotherapists have probably never even heard of her, this is a question the reader will doubtless want answered first. So here is a brief biographical summary.

She was born in Paris in 1908 into a devout Catholic family antipathetic to the prevailing laicist ideology of the Third Republic. Against the wishes of her parents, from whose expectations and outlook she struggled to extricate herself while retaining her religious allegiance, she trained as a doctor with a special interest in children.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Viviane Green and Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley  

This is a general edition of the Journal which reflects the theoretical interests of child psychotherapists. There is an original enlightening contribution from Anne Alvarez that re-claims sexuality as a key consideration in the work of child psychotherapists, as well as articles from Judith Mitrani and Graham Shulman which in turn explore new developments in neuroscience and chaos theory and their potential intersection with existing psychoanalytic ideas. The article by Claudia McLoughlin is an example of advancing a new model of psychoanalytic work outside the clinic setting and this together with the clinical commentary which features a six-year-old boy with a complicated background of disrupted care, testifies to the technical challenges faced by child psychotherapists in current practice.

Anne Alvarez's thought provoking paper, presented at the 2010 ACP conference, ‘Keeping the body in mind’, makes a lively and detailed plea for child psychotherapists to re-consider sexuality in the transference and countertransference. The need to reinstate the psychosexual aspects of psychoanalysis has recently been deemed important by a number of authors fearing that the recent emphasis on attachment and the real needs of developing infants seen through the eyes of child developmentalist research has perhaps obscured or under privileged psychosexuality. Alvarez's introduction reminds us of Freud's theories, the place of sexuality and aspects of sexuality which were perhaps missed; an affectionate, passionate drive, in the service of attachment and object relating: a precursor, Alvarez suggests to later adult sexuality.

The complexity of clinical work in the challenging environment of Pupil Referral Units, catering for disaffected and often violent children and adolescents who have been excluded from mainstream education, is the subject of the next article by McLoughlin. She makes a case for containment in concentric circles around the child, the family, the staff team of the Pupil Referral Unit and the wider multi-agency context. The psychotherapeutic frame in this unpredictable and unstable context, she argues, departs from the regular 50-minute session to be replaced by the psychotherapist's full and empathetic attention at every moment of encounter with these troubled children, however fragmented and brief the initial contact. From this embryonic beginning emerges the possibility of engaging some families in a more ‘traditional’ psychotherapeutic process as demonstrated by the clinical work she describes with one young adolescent and his mother.

This paper traces the analytic work with a severely traumatised two-and-a-half-year-old girl Phoebe, whose early life was marked by chronic abuse and a violent murder she witnessed a few months prior to the beginning of treatment. Bringing the trauma in the room in a dissociative form, in line with post-traumatic stress disorder presentation, was Phoebe's unconscious means of communicating her pre-verbal encounters by projecting onto me the rage, shock and helplessness of her predicament. Thus, countertransference responses were a helpful window into her internal world, which was governed by cataclysmic losses and primitive states of fear. The importance of containment of the complex feelings aroused in the work and protecting against potential re-enactment of the abusive elements the patient, the family and often the professional network brought in the therapy is highlighted. The author hopes that this paper will encourage the offering of psychoanalytic psychotherapy to traumatised children particularly the under fives.

Reparation by proxy: experiences of working with pregnant teenagers and adolescent mothers

Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley

120 Belsize Lane
London, NW3 5BA

Anne Hurley  

Adolescence, parenting, teenage pregnancy, separation, generational confusion, brief work, unresolved mourning

This paper describes brief work with pregnant teenagers, adolescent mothers, their infants and their wider families, a group who would not ordinarily seek treatment in child and adolescent mental health services. The work takes place in a community context in London and includes a home visiting service for young people unable to attend appointments in an advanced stage of pregnancy or in the early weeks of new motherhood. Accounts of emotional deprivation, disrupted care and separation in early childhood are often a feature of the history of many of these adolescents. Two case examples are considered in some detail. It is argued that for some young people, embarking on parenthood in adolescence is accompanied by the displaced attempt at repairing their own early relationships, as an alternative to the painful work of mourning.
